idea_html:
Count balanced numbers in [0, x] with a digit DP and answer f(high) − f(low − 1). Walk the digits of x left to right carrying five things: position, whether the prefix is still tight against x, whether a non-zero digit has started the number, the parity of the next position, and diff = odd-position sum − even-position sum. Leading zeros consume no position. At the end count 1 if started and diff == 0. Each class holds at most 8 digits, so diff stays in −72..72.

Sample 1, low = 1, high = 100. f(100) reads the string 100. First digit 0: not started, the remaining two digits form any number 0..99 — single digits have diff = d ≠ 0 (and 0 never starts), two-digit ab needs a − b = 0: 11, 22, …, 99, nine numbers. First digit 1: tight forces 100, diff = 1 − 0 + 0 = 1, not counted. f(100) = 9. f(0) returns 0. Answer 9.

States: 16 positions × 145 diffs × 2 tight × 2 started × 2 parity = 18,560, each trying ≤ 10 digits: about 2 × 105 operations per bound, so O(digits × 145 × 8 × 10) time and O(states) memory.
pitfalls_html:
• Loop from low to high and test each number. The range can hold 1015 numbers. Python checks about 106 per 0.92 s (measured on [1, 106]), so low = 1, high = 1015 needs roughly 29 years; even the manual's own "1.6 × 1016 ops at 109/s" is 1.6 × 107 s (185 days), not 18 million seconds. Two of the Python submissions in the record failed exactly this way.
  • One shared memo for both bounds. A cached tight state belongs to the digit string of the first call; reusing it for low − 1 returns counts for the wrong prefix. Ran it: low = 120, high = 129 gives 0 instead of 1, low = 11, high = 22 gives 0 instead of 2. Sample 1 still passes (f(0) returns before touching the cache), so the samples do not catch it. Build the memo inside f(x).
  • Believing leading zeros break the parity (the original manual's warning). They do not: a leading zero adds 0 to either sum, and shifting every position by one negates the alternating sum, which leaves diff == 0 unchanged. A DP over the zero-padded 16-digit string with no started flag matched brute force on 409 ranges. What padding does change is zero itself: 0000000000000000 has alternating sum 0, so f counts 0. That cancels in f(high) − f(low − 1) only if f(0) counts it too; add an early if x <= 0: return 0 and low = 1, high = 100 returns 10.
  • 32-bit counters. [1, 1015] holds 32,811,494,188,974 balanced numbers, 15,000 times 231 − 1. The Java solution below with int memo cells and totals returns −2,055,952,466 on low = 1, high = 1015 while still giving 55,251 on [1, 106] and passing all three samples.
changes: Tempting 3 ('Counting leading zeros as position 1 ... produces wrong counts for all values with fewer digits than x') is false: a leading zero adds 0 to either sum, and shifting every position's parity negates the alternating sum, which leaves 'sum equals 0' unchanged. A DP over the 16-digit zero-padded string with no started/parity flag matched brute force on 409 ranges <= 1e6.
Tempting 1 arithmetic: '1.6 x 10^16 operations ... even at 10^9 ops/sec this is 18 million seconds' - 1.6 x 10^16 / 10^9 = 1.6 x 10^7 = 16 million seconds (185 days).

Tempting 2 (one shared lru_cache across f(high) and f(low-1)) was asserted without an input; verified: low=120, high=129 returns 0 instead of 1, low=11, high=22 returns 0 instead of 2; sample 1 passes by accident because f(0) returns before the cache is used.

Essence 'Single-digit numbers are never balanced regardless of their value' is true only because of the two-digit rule: 0 alone has equal sums (0 = 0); a padded DP counts it and must count it consistently for both bounds.
